taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes Crother (2017) recognizes X. sierrae and X. wigginsi as separate species and that Papenfuss et al. (2001) split Arizona populations into X. vigilis, X. arizonae and X. bezyi, a change Stebbins (2003) did not adopt.
fieldMarks: Very small lizard (average adult total length about 8 cm, about 1.3 g) with soft granular scales on the back.
Grey, yellow-brownish or olive, often uniform but sometimes dark-spotted; can shift from light olive in the evening to dark brown by day.
Usually 12 longitudinal rows of rectangular ventral scales; males are lighter and shorter with a stouter tail and enlarged femoral pores.
Usually found under fallen yucca and Joshua tree logs or in rock-outcrop crevices rather than in the open.
behavior: Secretive: lives most of its life under cover, typically yucca logs, and is diurnal despite the name, sometimes active at night in summer.
Waits for termites, small beetles, ants, flies, spiders and other arthropods to wander by rather than actively searching.
Active from early April (low elevations) or May (higher) to late summer; gives live birth, about 2 young (1-3) in September-October.
Adult and young stay in family groups; groups of a few individuals aggregate under logs in winter.
habitat: Arid and semiarid habitats among fallen yucca, agave and Joshua tree logs, in rock crevices and under foothill pine bark, into pinyon-juniper, sagebrush-blackbrush and chaparral-oak; 300-2,070 m in California.
range: Southern Utah, western Arizona, southern Nevada and southern California south to southwestern Sonora and Baja California. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Arizona night lizard (Xantusia arizonae)
lookalikes.howToTell: Granite-adapted rather than yucca-dwelling; Arizona populations formerly called X. vigilis are now split among X. arizonae, X. bezyi and X. wigginsi.
